Midline brainstem cell groups that hold nearly all serotonin neurons; the dorsal and median raphe project forward to the forebrain and the caudal groups descend to the spinal cord.
Dense cluster of noradrenergic neurons in the dorsal pons that projects widely to cortex and hippocampus and fires with novel or attention-shifting stimuli.
Posterior hypothalamic cell group that is the brain's only source of neuronal histamine; it promotes wakefulness and is silent in REM sleep.
Rate-limiting enzyme of catecholamine synthesis, converting tyrosine to L-dopa; usually saturated, so extra tyrosine adds little dopamine.
Rate-limiting enzyme of serotonin synthesis; it is not saturated, so brain serotonin follows tryptophan supply.
VMAT; the transporter that loads monoamines into synaptic vesicles; reserpine blocks it and depletes monoamines.
Glutamate-gated ion channel that needs a co-agonist (glycine or D-serine) and depolarization to relieve its magnesium block; central to plasticity and excitotoxicity.
Co-agonist at the NMDA receptor glycine site, made by serine racemase and broken down by D-amino acid oxidase; low levels are linked to schizophrenia.
The view that weak NMDA signaling on cortical GABA interneurons disinhibits pyramidal cells and drives downstream dopamine excess in schizophrenia.
G protein-coupled GABA receptor that causes slow hyperpolarization through potassium channels; baclofen is its agonist.
A short chain of amino acids cut from a larger precursor that acts as a transmitter or modulator, usually through G protein-coupled receptors, and is cleared by peptidases rather than reuptake.
The large precursor protein, with a signal peptide, from which one or more active neuropeptides are cleaved.
TRH; hypothalamic tripeptide that releases pituitary TSH; a blunted TSH response to TRH is seen in some patients with depression.
CRF; hypothalamic peptide that drives ACTH release and coordinates the stress response; raised CSF levels are reported in depression.
Peptides of the CRF family (urocortin 1, 2 and 3) that act at CRF receptors; urocortin 1 is made mainly in the Edinger-Westphal nucleus.
Peptide that colocalizes with and modulates dopamine; it acts like an antipsychotic in animal tests and rises in mesolimbic regions with D2-blocking drugs.
Tachykinin peptide acting at NK1 receptors, involved in pain and stress; NK1 antagonists failed as antidepressants.
Signals such as nitric oxide and carbon monoxide that diffuse across membranes, are made on demand, are not stored in vesicles and have no surface receptor.
NOS; the enzyme that makes nitric oxide from arginine; the neuronal form (nNOS) is calcium-activated and coupled to NMDA receptors.
Enzyme that splits heme into carbon monoxide, free iron and biliverdin; heme oxygenase 2 is the main neuronal form.
Lipid signals such as anandamide and 2-AG that are made on demand from membrane lipids and act at cannabinoid receptors.
N-arachidonylethanolamine; an endocannabinoid that prefers CB1 receptors and is broken down mainly by fatty acid amide hydrolase.
2-AG; the most abundant brain endocannabinoid, acting at CB1 and CB2 alike and broken down mainly by monoacylglycerol lipase.
The main brain cannabinoid receptor, a G protein-coupled receptor on presynaptic terminals that reduces transmitter release.
Signaling from the postsynaptic cell back to the presynaptic terminal, as endocannabinoids do to suppress transmitter release.
FAAH; the enzyme that breaks down anandamide; blocking it raises anandamide, a strategy compared with MAO inhibition.
Essential polyunsaturated fatty acids with the first double bond three carbons from the methyl end, such as EPA and DHA; studied as add-on treatment in mood disorders.
